newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy's Marzotto calls off textile merger.
newsitem.headline: Italy's Marzotto calls off textile merger.

text.p: Italian textile group Marzotto has called off a merger with industrial holding HPI that would have created one of the biggest textiles and clothing companies in the world, the two firms said in a joint statement on Saturday.

The shock decision to scrap creation of an 8.24 trillion lire ($4.8 billion) group uniting a host of top names including German menswear label Hugo Boss, Giorgio Armani and sportswear maker Fila, was a blow to the Italian financial establishment.
Car maker Fiat and top Italian investment bank Mediobanca were to have held big stakes and Fiat chairman Cesare Romiti's son Maurizio was to have been managing director.
"The Marzotto board expressed with regret that circumstances have arisen which make the merger project inopportune," the joint statement said.

It said the board of Marzotto halted the deal with Holding Partecipazioni Industriali (HPI), a concern spun off from financial holding Gemina in March, "because incompatible differences have emerged".
HPI's board took note of the decision with regret, it said.

The groups, which had been due to hold shareholders' meetings this month ahead of share swaps in July that would have given birth to Gruppo Industriale Marzotto (GIM), failed to agree how the concern should be structured and run.

Problems emerged when the companies began preparatory work on the concrete details of the merger, the statement said. One particular sticking point was on financing and the recourse to risk capital and credit, it added.
GIM was to have been a clothing colossus with big interests in publishing and the backing of heavyweight Italian names.

Based on preliminary 1996 results, GIM would have had an estimated turnover of 8.24 trillion lire in 1996, a net profit of around 253 billion and more than 21,000 staff, the groups said when they announced the ambitious plan early in March.
That would have brought the two powerful competitors together in one of Italy's most important industrial holdings and analysts were initially upbeat, saying the deal looked good.

Besides clothing -- Marzotto owns Hugo Boss and HPI owns sportswear maker Fila and GFT, a textile group producing for top designers such as Giorgio Armani -- GIM would have owned Italy's second largest publisher, Rizzoli Corriere della Sera (RCS).
The groups said they would have had stakes in several other firms, and the cash resources to fund further investments.
Fiat was expected to have been the biggest shareholder with a 17.3 percent stake, followed by the Marzotto family with 12.4 percent and Mediobanca with 10 percent.

Analysts said they saw the hand of Mediobanca's 90-year-old honorary chairman Enrico Cuccia, the grand old man of Italian finance, at work in the HPI-Marzotto deal, which was to have succeeded where the collapse of a former mega-merger failed.
Instead, Cuccia appeared to have lost his Midas touch.
The HPI-Marzotto merger followed the collapse of the so-called "SuperGemina" deal, originated by Cuccia in late 1995, to bundle Gemina's interests with the former Ferruzzi agri-chemicals empire.
After the deal was abandoned, following the discovery of huge losses at RCS, Ferruzzi was renamed Compart and Gemina's core interests hived off into HPI. ($1-1,711)
